cim: Getting Started with Docker for Machine Learning and MLOps
cim_eredeti: Getting Started with Docker for Machine Learning and MLOps
szoveg_eredeti:
In this lesson, we will learn how to use Docker for MLOps, starting with why Docker matters in machine learning (ML), then exploring Docker fundamentals and architecture, running basic Docker commands, building reproducible ML environments, and containerizing an ML project. We will also cover best practices for ML images, finish with a hands-on exercise, and briefly look at some popular Docker alternatives.

This lesson is the 2nd in a 3-part series on Machine Learning Operations (MLOps):

To learn how to use Docker for MLOps, from fundamentals and commands to best practices and containerizing your first ML project, just keep reading.

A common phrase in machine learning is “It works on my machine.” That is because ML projects are uniquely fragile. A model that runs fine on a laptop may fail completely on a production server.

Why does this happen? Machine learning brings extra challenges:

For traditional software, these mismatches are frustrating. For ML, they are crippling. Reproducibility requires consistency in both research and production.

Docker solves this by letting you package code, dependencies, drivers, and configuration into a container image. That image runs the same way everywhere: on a laptop, on a teammate’s machine, or inside a Kubernetes cluster.

A Real Example: Imagine a PyTorch model is trained locally with PyTorch 2.2 + CUDA 12.1. The production server, however, has PyTorch 2.1 + CUDA 11.8. When you try to deploy, your code fails because the CUDA kernels do not match. The result? Debugging hell, wasted hours, and frustrated teammates.

Now enter Docker. With Docker, we package our code, dependencies, and runtime into a container image. This image provides a consistent software environment across compatible hosts in development and production. The CUDA runtime travels with the code. The server still needs a compatible NVIDIA driver.

In the context of MLOps, Docker is not just a convenience. It is the foundation. MLOps requires reproducibility, scalability, and collaboration. If experiments cannot be reproduced, deployment cannot be trusted, and monitoring and retraining are meaningless. Docker makes reproducibility and portability non-negotiable, which is why every modern ML pipeline starts here.

To follow this guide, you only need Docker installed on your system. That is it!

The beauty of containerization is that all Python dependencies (e.g., PyTorch and Lightning) are installed inside the container, so the host machine does not need them.

That is all you need! The container handles everything else. Python, PyTorch, datasets, and dependencies are all managed inside the isolated environment.

Before we start running commands, it is important to understand what Docker actually is and how it works under the hood. Many new ML engineers use Docker without really grasping its fundamentals, but in MLOps, a clear mental model will save countless hours of debugging later.

At a glance, containers and virtual machines (VMs) may look similar. Both isolate applications so they can run in their own environments. But there is a crucial difference:

Analogy: Think of a VM as a full house with its own foundation, walls, plumbing, and electricity. A container is more like a furnished apartment in a building. It is lighter, starts faster, and is easier to move.

This efficiency is one reason Docker became so popular in machine learning. We can spin up lightweight, isolated environments quickly without waiting minutes for a VM to boot.

Docker follows a client–server architecture. When we type commands (e.g., docker run or docker build), we interact with the Docker client, which communicates with the Docker daemon.

Workflow Example: When we run docker run hello-world, the client sends the request to the daemon. The daemon checks whether the image exists locally and pulls it from a registry if needed. It then creates and runs a container from the image.

⚠️ Common error: If we see Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock. Is the docker daemon running?, it means the client cannot talk to the daemon. This usually happens if Docker Desktop (on macOS or Windows) is not running or the Docker service (on Linux) has not started.

While Docker remains one of the most widely adopted container platforms, alternatives are gaining traction. Podman, backed by Red Hat, offers a daemonless architecture and supports running containers without root privileges. It is also compatible with Docker-built images that follow the Open Container Initiative (OCI) image standard. We will stick with Docker throughout this course, but it is useful to be aware of the broader container ecosystem.

With these fundamentals in mind, we can see how Docker uses a client–server architecture to run lightweight, portable containers from images that can be distributed through registries.

Instead, it uses the instructions in the Dockerfile to build a Docker image. When we run that image, Docker creates and starts a container from it.
